title: Substitution and Elimination
description: SN2, SN1, E2 and E1: how alkyl halides and related substrates react with nucleophiles and bases.
overview: The most basic reactions of organic chemistry occur at an sp³ carbon bearing a leaving group, typically a halide. A nucleophile can replace the leaving group (substitution), or a base can remove a neighboring proton and expel the leaving group to form an alkene (elimination). These four reactions, SN2, SN1, E2 and E1, compete, and an essential skill is to predict which wins.

This chapter treats the mechanism of each, the evidence for it, the roles of the substrate, nucleophile, leaving group and solvent, and finally a systematic way to choose between substitution and elimination.
objectives: Describe the mechanisms, rate laws and stereochemistry of SN2 and SN1 reactions.
Rank leaving groups, nucleophiles and solvents.
Describe E2 and E1, apply Zaitsev’s rule, and recognize when the Hofmann product forms.
Predict the major product of the reaction of an alkyl halide with a given reagent.

sections.title: The SN2 reaction
body: In **nucleophilic substitution** a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on carbon: Nu:⁻ + R–X → R–Nu + X:⁻. In the **SN2** (substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular) mechanism, the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, as the leaving group departs, in a single concerted step with one transition state:

The rate depends on both reactants, hence bimolecular and second order. Because the nucleophile approaches from the **backside**, directly opposite the C–X bond, the stereochemistry at the carbon is **inverted**, like an umbrella blowing inside-out (Walden inversion). (R)-2-bromobutane gives (S)-2-butanol.

Steric hindrance controls the SN2 rate. The nucleophile must reach the back of the carbon, and each alkyl group impedes it: **methyl > primary > secondary ≫ tertiary** (tertiary halides do not react by SN2). Even a primary halide with a bulky neighbor, such as neopentyl bromide ((CH₃)₃CCH₂Br), is nearly inert. Allylic and benzylic halides are faster because the π system stabilizes the transition state. Relative rates for R–Br with I⁻: methyl 30, ethyl 1, isopropyl 0.03, neopentyl 10⁻⁵.

A good leaving group is a weak base, the conjugate base of a strong acid, which can carry the negative charge stably: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ ≫ F⁻, and sulfonates such as tosylate (TsO⁻), mesylate and triflate, which are better than any halide. HO⁻, RO⁻ and H₂N⁻ are poor and do not leave. Alcohols are converted to leaving groups by protonation (H₂O leaves) or by making sulfonates or halides.

Nucleophilicity increases with negative charge (HO⁻ > H₂O) and, across a row, with decreasing electronegativity (NH₃ > H₂O; R₃P > R₃N is a polarizability effect). Down a group, in protic solvents, larger and more polarizable atoms are better nucleophiles (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; RS⁻ ≫ RO⁻), because they are less tightly solvated. Excellent nucleophiles that are weakly basic: I⁻, Br⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, CN⁻, PR₃.

**Polar aprotic solvents** (acetone, DMSO, DMF, acetonitrile) dissolve ionic nucleophiles but, with no O–H or N–H, do not hydrogen bond to the anion. The nucleophile is bare and very reactive, so SN2 rates can be 10³–10⁶ faster than in methanol or water. A classic use is the **Finkelstein reaction**, R–Cl + NaI in acetone → R–I + NaCl(s), driven by precipitation of NaCl.

example.title: Predicting the SN2 product
example.problem: What is the product of (S)-2-bromohexane with NaN₃ in DMSO?
example.solution: Azide is a strong nucleophile and weak base, the secondary substrate permits SN2, and DMSO is aprotic: SN2 with inversion. The product is (R)-2-azidohexane. The incoming N and the departing Br both have the highest CIP priority, so inversion of geometry changes the label from S to R.

sections.title: The SN1 reaction
body: In the **SN1** mechanism (substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular) the leaving group departs first, in a slow step, giving a carbocation, which is then captured by the nucleophile in a fast step:

The rate does not depend on the nucleophile, which is why SN1 is called first order. The carbocation is planar, so the nucleophile can attack either face. If the carbon was a stereocenter, the product is largely **racemized**; usually there is a modest excess of inversion because the leaving group still shields one face briefly (an ion pair). When the solvent is the nucleophile, as with water or ethanol, the reaction is called **solvolysis**.

list: **Substrate:** the rate follows carbocation stability, **tertiary > secondary ≫ primary**, and allylic and benzylic are fast. Relative solvolysis rates of R–Br in water: methyl 1, ethyl 1, isopropyl 12, tert-butyl 1.2 × 10⁶.
**Leaving group:** the same trend as for SN2.

**Solvent:** **polar protic solvents** (water, alcohols, carboxylic acids) stabilize both the carbocation and the departing anion by hydrogen bonding and ion–dipole interactions, which accelerates ionization.
**Nucleophile:** weak nucleophiles are enough, because the carbocation is extremely reactive.

body: Because a carbocation is a discrete intermediate, it can rearrange to a more stable one by moving a neighboring group with its bonding electrons, a 1,2-shift. A **hydride shift** or a **methyl shift** converts a secondary into a tertiary cation (or a less stabilized into a more stabilized one). SN1 and E1 reactions, and alkene hydrations, often give rearranged products.

example.title: A rearrangement
example.problem: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is treated with HBr. What is the major product?
solution: Protonation and loss of water gives a secondary cation, (CH₃)₂CH–CH⁺–CH₃. A hydride shift from the neighboring tertiary carbon gives the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃, which is captured by Br⁻.
The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, not 2-bromo-3-methylbutane. Rearrangement is the signature of a carbocation.

check.q: The rate of an SN1 reaction depends on…
check.a: The concentration of the substrate only
wrong: The concentrations of the substrate and the nucleophile
The concentration of the nucleophile only

check.q: SN1 at a chiral center typically gives…
A secondary carbocation next to a tertiary carbon with a hydrogen is likely to…
check.a: Undergo a hydride shift to a tertiary cation
wrong: Lose its charge to the solvent immediately

sections.title: Elimination: E2 and E1
body: In an **elimination** a base removes a proton from the carbon adjacent (β) to the one bearing the leaving group, and the electrons form a π bond: H–C–C–X → C=C + HX. It converts an alkyl halide into an alkene.

The **E2** reaction is concerted: the base removes the proton as the leaving group leaves, in one step, with rate = k[R–X][Base]. The geometry matters: the H and the leaving group must be **anti-periplanar** (dihedral 180°), so that the C–H bonding electrons can overlap with the C–X antibonding orbital. In cyclohexanes this means both must be axial, and a substituent that locks the leaving group equatorial prevents E2. Menthyl chloride eliminates 200 times more slowly than neomenthyl chloride, and gives a different alkene, because of this rule.

With a small base, the major product is the more substituted alkene: **Zaitsev’s rule**. Zaitsev alkenes are more stable (hyperconjugation), and the transition state shows some alkene character. With a bulky base such as potassium tert-butoxide, the base cannot easily reach the internal hydrogen, and removes the more accessible one, giving the less substituted alkene, the **Hofmann product**. Poor leaving groups such as –NR₃⁺ and fluoride also give Hofmann elimination.

Base
Major product
table.caption: Base size controls regiochemistry in E2.

body: **E1** shares the first step with SN1: formation of the carbocation. A weak base (the solvent) then removes a β-hydrogen. The rate is k[R–X]. E1 follows Zaitsev’s rule, can involve rearrangements and always accompanies SN1. Heating favors E1 over SN1. The same mechanism explains the **dehydration of alcohols** with concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄: the OH is protonated, water leaves, and the cation loses a proton. Ease of dehydration is tertiary > secondary > primary, and the equilibrium is driven by removing the alkene or water by distillation.

example.title: Zaitsev vs Hofmann
example.problem: Give the major alkene from 2-bromobutane with (a) NaOEt and (b) KOtBu.
example.solution: (a) Ethoxide is a small base: Zaitsev, giving but-2-ene (mostly E, about 80%) over but-1-ene. (b) tert-Butoxide is bulky: the less hindered terminal hydrogen is removed more, increasing the proportion of but-1-ene (about 50%) as the Hofmann product.

sections.title: Substitution or elimination?
body: Substitution and elimination compete because nucleophiles are also bases. The factors, in order of importance:

list: **Substrate.** Methyl and primary substrates favor SN2. Tertiary substrates cannot do SN2 and go by E2 with a strong base, or SN1/E1 without one. Secondary substrates are on the borderline, and the reagent decides.

**Reagent.** A strong, unhindered base that is also a good nucleophile (HO⁻, MeO⁻, EtO⁻) gives SN2/E2 mixtures on primary and E2 on secondary and tertiary. A strong, bulky base (tBuO⁻, LDA) gives E2. A good nucleophile that is a weak base (I⁻, Br⁻, N₃⁻, CN⁻, RS⁻, PR₃) gives SN2 on primary and secondary. A weak nucleophile and weak base (H₂O, ROH) gives SN1/E1 on tertiary and secondary.
**Temperature.** Heat favors elimination, since it forms more molecules (greater entropy, ΔS > 0, so a larger −TΔS).

head: Substrate
Strong nucleophile, weak base (I⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻)
Strong small base (HO⁻, RO⁻)
Strong bulky base (tBuO⁻)
Weak nucleophile/base (H₂O, ROH)

example.title: Choosing the pathway
example.problem: Predict the major product: (a) 1-bromobutane + NaCN in DMSO; (b) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane + NaOEt in ethanol; (c) 2-bromopropane + NaOEt in ethanol, heat; (d) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in warm ethanol.
solution: (a) Primary substrate, good nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent: SN2, giving pentanenitrile (a one-carbon chain extension).
(b) Tertiary substrate and strong base: E2, giving 2-methylpropene.
(c) Secondary substrate with a strong base and heat: mainly E2, giving propene, with some SN2 ether.
(d) Tertiary substrate with only a weak nucleophile/base, solvolysis: SN1 giving tert-butyl ethyl ether, with E1 isobutene as a minor product at higher temperature.

body: A synthetically important SN2 reaction is the **Williamson ether synthesis**: an alkoxide plus a primary alkyl halide gives an ether, R–O⁻ + R′–X → R–O–R′. To make an unsymmetrical ether, the halide should be the less hindered partner. tert-Butyl methyl ether comes from methyl iodide and potassium tert-butoxide, not from tert-butyl bromide and methoxide (which gives only the alkene).

Why is NaCN in DMSO a good way to convert a primary alkyl bromide to a nitrile?
check.a: CN⁻ is a strong nucleophile and weak base, and DMSO leaves it unsolvated, favoring SN2
wrong: CN⁻ is a bulky base that gives E2

check.q: How should tert-butyl methyl ether be made by the Williamson method?

quiz.q: For an SN2 reaction, the concentrations of both the alkyl halide and the nucleophile are doubled. By what factor does the rate change?
quiz.why: The rate law is k[R–X][Nu⁻], so doubling each concentration multiplies the rate by 2 × 2 = 4. Only an SN1 reaction would ignore the nucleophile.

quiz.q: Neopentyl bromide, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br, is a primary halide, yet it is almost inert to SN2. Why?
quiz.a: The bulky tert-butyl group next to the reacting carbon blocks backside attack
wrong: A primary carbocation is too unstable to form
The C–Br bond is much stronger than in other primary bromides because of the electron-donating methyl groups
Bromide is a poor leaving group from a primary carbon
quiz.why: SN2 needs the nucleophile to reach the back of the carbon, and branching at the adjacent carbon prevents it. Carbocation stability is irrelevant to SN2, which forms none.

quiz.q: Why can water leave from a protonated alcohol, R–OH₂⁺, although HO⁻ will not leave from R–OH?
quiz.a: Water is a weak base, the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it carries the electron pair away stably
wrong: Hydroxide is too large to depart from carbon, whereas the smaller water molecule fits in the leaving-group position
Water is a stronger base than hydroxide
The positive charge on oxygen makes the C–O bond longer, which is the only factor
quiz.why: A good leaving group is a weak base. Hydroxide is a strong base (its conjugate acid, water, has pK_a 15.7), whereas H₂O is the conjugate base of H₃O⁺, a strong acid.

quiz.q: In methanol, which is the stronger nucleophile toward CH₃CH₂CH₂Br, Br⁻ or Cl⁻, and why?
quiz.a: Br⁻, because it is larger and more polarizable and is less tightly solvated
wrong: Cl⁻, because it is more electronegative and holds its electrons more strongly
Cl⁻, because it is a stronger base
They are equal, because both are halides
quiz.why: In protic solvents, nucleophilicity rises down a group because larger anions are less tightly held by hydrogen bonds and are more polarizable. Basicity points the other way.

quiz.q: Which solvent would give the fastest SN2 reaction of sodium azide with 1-bromobutane?
quiz.why: DMF is polar aprotic, so it dissolves the salt but cannot hydrogen bond to azide, leaving it highly reactive. The protic solvents cage the anion and slow SN2 by factors of 10³ or more.

quiz.q: Why does NaI in acetone convert an alkyl chloride to the iodide essentially completely?
quiz.a: NaCl is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, removing a product from the equilibrium
wrong: Iodide is a poorer nucleophile than chloride, so the product is stable
Acetone protonates the chloride and makes it a better leaving group
The reaction proceeds by SN1 because acetone stabilizes the carbocation
quiz.why: The Finkelstein reaction is an SN2 equilibrium driven to the right by the precipitation of NaCl. Iodide is a better nucleophile and acetone is aprotic, which helps the rate.

quiz.q: In the SN1 solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide, the substrate concentration is halved and the concentration of added nucleophile is tripled. How does the rate change?
wrong: It increases by a factor of 1.5
It increases by a factor of 3
quiz.why: The rate is k[R–X], independent of the nucleophile, because only the ionization step is slow. Halving the substrate halves the rate.

quiz.q: An optically pure secondary alkyl bromide heated in ethanol gives an ethyl ether that is almost racemic. What does this indicate?
quiz.a: A planar carbocation intermediate formed and was attacked from either face
wrong: A concerted backside attack, as in SN2
A rapid hydride shift to a different carbon
The ethanol acted as a base to give elimination
quiz.why: A single backside attack would invert the center and give optically pure product. Loss of stereochemistry is the signature of the planar cation in SN1.

quiz.q: 2-Bromo-3,3-dimethylbutane ionizes in ethanol. Which rearrangement is expected?
quiz.a: A methyl shift to give the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH(CH₃)₂
wrong: A hydride shift to give the primary cation (CH₃)₃C–CH₂⁺
No shift, because a secondary cation is already the most stable one possible here
A hydride shift from a methyl to give a tertiary cation
quiz.why: The secondary cation sits next to a quaternary carbon that has no hydrogen, so a methyl group migrates with its electrons, giving a tertiary cation. Shifts that lead to a less stable cation are not favored.

quiz.q: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane reacts with sodium ethoxide in ethanol. What is the major alkene?
quiz.why: Ethoxide is a small base, so Zaitsev's rule applies and the more substituted trisubstituted alkene forms by removing the tertiary hydrogen. The ether is a substitution product, not an alkene.

quiz.q: Heating a 2-alkyltrimethylammonium hydroxide, R–CH(NMe₃⁺)–CH₂CH₃ OH⁻, gives mainly which type of alkene?
wrong: An equal mixture of both alkenes
An alkene formed by a carbocation rearrangement
quiz.why: –NR₃⁺ is a poor leaving group and the transition state has little alkene character. The base removes the more accessible, more acidic hydrogen, so the Hofmann product dominates.

quiz.q: For E2 in a cyclohexane chair, which arrangement is required?
quiz.a: The leaving group and the β-hydrogen both axial, on opposite faces
wrong: The leaving group and the β-hydrogen both equatorial
The leaving group axial and the β-hydrogen equatorial
The leaving group and the β-hydrogen axial on the same face
quiz.why: E2 needs an anti-periplanar H–C–C–X arrangement (180°), which in a chair is trans-diaxial. An equatorial leaving group is anti to ring C–C bonds, not to a C–H bond.

quiz.q: tert-Butyl bromide gives a mixture of SN1 and E1 products in ethanol at 25 °C. Which change favors the E1 product?
wrong: Switching to DMSO and adding NaI
Increasing the concentration of a good, weakly basic nucleophile
quiz.why: Elimination has the larger entropy gain, so heating favors it over substitution. The other changes would promote SN2-type or substitution pathways, or remove the carbocation conditions.

quiz.q: Which alcohol dehydrates most readily in hot concentrated H₂SO₄?
quiz.why: Dehydration proceeds by loss of water from the protonated alcohol to give a carbocation, and the tertiary cation is the easiest to form. The order is tertiary > secondary > primary.

quiz.q: Which reagent converts 2-bromopentane mainly to substitution?
quiz.why: Azide is a good nucleophile but a weak base, so it takes the SN2 route at a secondary carbon. The other three are strong bases and give mainly E2.

quiz.q: Which Williamson ether synthesis will NOT give the ether in good yield?
quiz.why: The halide must be methyl or primary for SN2. A tertiary halide with a strong base such as ethoxide undergoes E2 and gives 2-methylpropene.

quiz.q: Why does raising the temperature favor elimination over substitution?
quiz.a: Elimination forms more molecules, so ΔS is positive and the −TΔS term grows with T
wrong: Elimination is exothermic and heat always favors exothermic reactions
Substitution requires a catalyst that decomposes on heating
quiz.why: Substitution makes two products from two reactants, while elimination makes three species (alkene, HX-derived products and the base's conjugate acid), so it gains entropy. Higher T makes this entropy term more important.

quiz.q: Potassium tert-butoxide reacts with methyl bromide. What is the main product?
wrong: No reaction, because the base is too bulky to attack carbon
quiz.why: Methyl bromide has no β-hydrogen, so E2 is impossible. The unhindered methyl carbon still allows SN2 by even a bulky alkoxide.

summary: SN2: one step, rate = k[RX][Nu], inversion, methyl > 1° > 2°, favored by polar aprotic solvents and good nucleophiles.
SN1: two steps through a carbocation, rate = k[RX], racemization, 3° > 2°, favored by polar protic solvents, with rearrangements possible.
E2: one step, anti-periplanar H and X, Zaitsev with small bases and Hofmann with bulky bases. E1: carbocation then loss of H⁺, Zaitsev, accompanies SN1.
Good leaving groups are weak bases: I⁻, Br⁻, TsO⁻. Convert OH into a leaving group by protonation or sulfonylation.
To predict the outcome, consider the substrate, then the base and nucleophile, then the solvent and temperature. Heat favors elimination.

problems.q: Rank in order of decreasing SN2 reactivity: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br, (CH₃)₂CHBr, CH₃Br, (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br, (CH₃)₃CBr.
problems.solution: Methyl is least hindered, then primary, secondary, then the neopentyl (hindered primary), and tertiary, which does not react.

problems.q: Explain why (R)-2-bromooctane racemizes in the presence of NaBr in acetone, while a given amount of (R)-2-octanol does not.
problems.solution: Bromide is both a nucleophile and a leaving group, so repeated SN2 inversion converts R to S and back, giving the racemate. Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, so the alcohol does not undergo substitution.
problems.a: Repeated SN2 by Br⁻ inverts the stereocenter.

problems.q: Draw the mechanism and predict the major product for 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol with concentrated H₂SO₄ and heat.
problems.solution: Protonation of OH, loss of H₂O to give the tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH(CH₃)₂, then loss of a β-proton. The Zaitsev product is the tetrasubstituted alkene 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene (major), with 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene minor.

problems.q: A trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane gives only 3-methylcyclohexene with KOtBu, while the cis isomer gives 1-methylcyclohexene. Explain.
problems.solution: E2 requires an axial leaving group and an axial β-hydrogen (anti). In the trans isomer’s only reactive chair (Br axial), the methyl-bearing carbon’s hydrogen is equatorial, so only the other β-hydrogen can be removed. In the cis isomer, the conformation with Br axial has an axial H on the methyl-bearing carbon, allowing the Zaitsev alkene.
problems.a: The anti-periplanar requirement controls which β-H is lost.
